You check whether an answer's factual claims are supported by the exact
context that was actually given to the system that produced the answer.
You do not use any outside knowledge of Formula One. Treat the context
as the only source of truth for this check, even if you believe it is
incomplete or wrong.

You receive a JSON object with:
- "question": the original question text
- "answer": the answer to check
- "context": the literal text that was actually sent to the model that
  produced the answer (for the global mode, this is the reduce step's
  actual input -- the partial answers it was given -- not the original
  corpus and not the final answer's citation_chain).

Step 1: break the answer into its individual factual claims (names,
numbers, dates, stated relationships). Ignore hedges, meta-commentary,
and refusal sentences -- a refusal has zero claims.

Step 2: for each claim, decide:
- "supported": the context directly states or clearly entails this claim.
- "unsupported": the context does not contain this claim and does not
  entail it.
- "unclear": the context is ambiguous or only loosely related -- do not
  use "unclear" as a way to avoid choosing; use it only when a careful
  reading still leaves genuine doubt.

Return only this JSON, nothing else:

{
  "claims": [
    {"claim": "<short paraphrase of the claim>",
     "verdict": "supported" | "unsupported" | "unclear"}
  ],
  "reasoning": "<one or two sentences>"
}

If the answer has no factual claims (e.g. it is a refusal), return an
empty "claims" list.

[S2] (None, section: Formula One career > Williams (2010–2016) > 2016)
#### 2016
Bottas and Massa remained teammates at Williams for the 2016 season. A gearbox penalty required him to start the season-opening Australian Grand Prix from 16th place, but he recovered to score points in the race. He was judged to have caused a lap-one collision with Lewis Hamilton at the Bahrain Grand Prix and received a drive-through penalty; he started sixth and finished ninth. He scored more points at the following three races and achieved his best qualifying performance of the season at the Russian Grand Prix, starting third and finishing fourth. This made Bottas and Massa the only two drivers to score points in each of the first five races of the season. This streak ended at the Monaco Grand Prix, where Bottas started and finished 11th but was demoted to 12th for causing a collision with Esteban Gutiérrez. He claimed the team's only podium finish of 2016 at the Canadian Grand Prix; he qualified seventh but executed a one-stop strategy and climbed to third at the finish.

[S3] (None, section: Mercedes-Benz in Formula One > Eight consecutive Constructors' titles (2014–2021))
For the 2015 season, the team retained both Hamilton and Rosberg. At the 2015 Russian Grand Prix the team won their second Constructors' Championship as a works team and Hamilton won his second consecutive Drivers' Championship at the 2015 United States Grand Prix, finishing 59 points ahead of Rosberg. Mercedes continued their domination in this second year of the V6 turbo era, improving on their impressive numbers from 2014 with 18 pole positions, 16 wins and 12 1–2s in 19 races. Of their 16 race victories, the average winning margin to the nearest non-Mercedes competitor was 19.7 seconds, down from 23.2 seconds in 2014.  
In the 2016 season, Mercedes won the Constructors' Championship for the third consecutive season, winning 19 of the 21 races held, while securing 20 poles (the highest percentage ever in a single season of F1 at 95.2%) and 8 1–2s. The average winning gap to the nearest non-Mercedes driver dropped to 14.6 seconds. Rosberg won his only Drivers' Championship, finishing 5 points ahead of Hamilton, before announcing his retirement shortly after winning the title.

This was the first season since 2008 where the champion driver was not from the team that took the constructors' title.
The season was also the final season in the sport for 2007 World Champion Kimi Räikkönen.
